title: Wandering isn't all bad
hookLine: mind-wandering also helps planning and creativity (Smallwood and Schooler)

cards: A shower, hot water, nothing to do but stand there. And out of nowhere comes the answer to the problem that wouldn't budge all afternoon. The name that wouldn't come.
The right first sentence of the email. The mind wandered off, and came back carrying something. This week has treated the wandering mind a little like a runaway dog: catch it, bring it back.
That's real, but it isn't the whole story. Today, the case for the wandering mind.

teach.b: William James described thought as a stream: "It is nothing jointed; it flows." Streams wander; that's what they do.
The psychologists Jonathan Smallwood and Jonathan Schooler study where the stream goes when it leaves the task, and their review is honest on both sides.
The costs are real: wander while reading and the page doesn't stay; wander while driving or listening and something gets missed. But there are benefits too.
A drifting mind often drifts toward the future: planning, rehearsing, working out what to do next.
And in one study they discuss, people stuck on a creative problem did better after a break on an easy task that let the mind roam than after a break on a hard one.
So the mind in the shower may have been working the whole time. Here's what ties this to the week: what seems to matter isn't only whether the mind wanders, but whether we know it's wandering.
Researchers call this meta-awareness, noticing where attention is. A mind that drifts without noticing gets lost on the road. A mind that drifts and knows it's drifting is out for a walk.
Look back at the week's lines: monks and scientists, bring it back, what am I missing, a little at a time, the idling mind. Every one is about noticing.
Today adds the other half: sometimes, once you notice, you let it go on purpose.

how: Researchers study mind-wandering by interrupting people at random moments during a task and asking where their attention was and whether they knew it had drifted; some meditation traditions include periods of open, unguided sitting alongside focused practice.

games.q: what does “wandering isn't all bad” mean?
o: daydreaming is only useful while you are asleep
letting the mind drift always ruins the work at hand
a drifting mind can plan and find answers, if noticed

games.q: the case for wandering: tap the pairs.
p: it is nothing jointed; it flows

s: research shows mind-wandering is always harmful
the costs are real, but wandering also helps with planning and, in some studies, creative problems.
a wandering mind often drifts toward the future
planning, rehearsing, working out what to do next.
one thing that seems to matter is whether we know the mind is wandering

games.q: you're stuck on a creative problem and need a break. in the study Smallwood and Schooler discuss, which break helped more?
o: a hard task that kept the mind fully busy.
an easy task that let the mind roam.
no break; keep grinding at the problem.
games.why: the easy task. people who came back from a break that let the mind wander did better on the problems they'd already met.

practice: Give the mind one loose direction, a problem you've been stuck on or the week ahead, then stop steering and let it drift, like a dog off the leash in an open field.
Keep only a light eye on it, oh, it's gone to last Tuesday, oh, now it's planning dinner, and don't bring it back; just know where it is.

wordCard.voice: Wandering isn't all bad. A drifting mind can plan and find answers, especially when it knows it's drifting. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: wander on purpose. A mind that knows it's drifting is out for a walk. That ends this week.
